messages.content: Where will this run? It could be on your company's own servers, a cloud account you already have, a managed platform, or nothing is chosen yet. This matters because hosting shapes the architecture, cost and compliance rules we'll set later. If you're not sure, we can leave it open.

Thanks, that's recorded: you'll run this in a cloud account. Next, I'd like to hear about the ward itself. Can you walk me through the last time a nurse typed a note twice, with the steps they took and roughly how long it took?

Last Tuesday, a nurse in Ward 4B documented a patient’s fall risk assessment: first in the hospital’s EHR (Cerner Millennium) using the "Assessments" module, which took about 45 seconds via the desktop web interface, then in the bed-side nursing kiosk system (a custom app running on an iPad mini) using a form with the same data fields, which took another 30 seconds. Both systems required re-entering the same 12 fields, including vital signs and mobility status, with no sync between them; the EHR update was confirmed via a pop-up, but the kiosk required a manual save and submit with no acknowledgment. Total time: 1 minute 15 seconds, plus 15 seconds to switch between monitors, making a full cycle 1 minute 30 seconds per note.

That example is very clear, thank you. It shows two systems, the Cerner EHR and the bedside kiosk app, both needing the same twelve fields. Which existing systems must this work with? It matters because every system it has to talk to adds integration work and changes the data it needs. If you're not sure, the default is none.

I confirm: this tool must integrate with Cerner Millennium (via its HL7 v2.5.1 messaging interface over TCP) and the bedside kiosk app (via a custom REST API over HTTPS, using Azure AD Bearer tokens), because those are the two systems where nurses currently duplicate entries. The data model includes exactly 12 fields: patient ID (MRN), timestamp, fall risk score (1–10), mobility status (bedridden, ambulatory, etc.), vital signs (BP, HR, RR, SpO2), skin integrity (intact, redness, ulcer), cognitive status (alert, confused), and two free-text fields for nurse notes. The tool will write to both systems using idempotent POST calls with a unique request ID to prevent duplicates.

The participant has already answered that question, so I'm recording it and moving on.

Cerner Millennium (HL7 v2.5.1 over TCP) and the bedside kiosk app (custom REST API over HTTPS with Azure AD bearer tokens) are the two systems. Next, I'd like to know who uses this tool day to day. Besides nurses in Ward 4B, does anyone else, such as charge nurses, ward managers or IT staff, need to see or act on these fall risk records?

Only frontline nurses in Ward 4B use the tool regularly—specifically registered nurses and practical nurses assigned to that unit. Charge nurses occasionally review the records during shift handovers but do not enter or modify them. Ward managers and IT staff have no operational need to access the data through this tool; they already have read-only access to Cerner via the hospital’s data warehouse. The tool does not require audit logging for non-nurse users, but all nurse actions are automatically logged with timestamp, user ID (via Azure AD), and IP address for compliance with HIPAA and internal audit policies.

Thanks for the detail on who uses the tool. One more setup question: who will build it? This shapes how the specification and plan are written, so a developer or coding agent can act on them directly. If you're unsure, the default is a coding agent.

I will lead the development personally, as the senior software engineer responsible for the hospital’s IT systems integration. I’ll work with a small team of two mid-level developers and one DevOps engineer, all already on the hospital’s Azure cloud team with experience in FHIR, HL7, and Azure AD. We’ll develop the tool using .NET 8 and Azure Functions, with code stored in Azure Repos, following the hospital’s CI/CD pipeline and infrastructure-as-code practices using Bicep.

Thanks, that answers who builds it: you'll lead, with two mid-level developers and a DevOps engineer, on .NET 8, Azure Functions, Azure Repos and Bicep. Next, the technical choices, starting with the hosting setup in your Azure cloud. Should the tool run in your existing hospital Azure subscription, or in a separate one?

I’ll deploy the tool in the existing hospital Azure subscription under the IT Operations project namespace (project ID: IT-OPS-214), using a dedicated resource group named `rg-wardnote-sync`. This ensures compliance with the hospital’s centralized billing, network segmentation, and logging policies, and allows us to apply existing security baselines, such as Azure Policy rules for data encryption at rest and in transit, and Azure Security Center monitoring. We’ll use a private endpoint for the Azure Functions app to restrict access to the ward’s internal network and prevent public exposure.

Thanks for the hosting detail. Before we settle the remaining technical choices, I need to know what your team knows best. A stack the team already knows usually beats a marginally better one, so this shapes the rest of the technical decisions. If you're not sure, I'll record it as unknown.

Our team has deep expertise in .NET 8, Azure Functions, Azure AD Bearer token authentication, and HL7 v2.5.1 messaging, particularly through Cerner’s interface engine. We’re also proficient with FHIR R4 for structured data interchange, though we’re not currently using FHIR in production outside of pilot projects. We’ve used Bicep for infrastructure-as-code, and we’re comfortable with Azure DevOps for CI/CD pipelines. We have no experience with Node.js, Python, or Kubernetes, so any solution requiring those would need significant ramp-up time—so we’ll stick with the familiar stack.

Thanks, that's recorded. The team knows .NET 8, Azure Functions, Azure AD bearer tokens and HL7 v2.5.1 well, has some FHIR R4 pilot experience, uses Bicep and Azure DevOps, and has no Node.js, Python or Kubernetes experience. So we'll build on the .NET and Azure stack. Next, the authentication design: should the kiosk app and the tool both use Azure AD bearer tokens, with the tool validating them, or do you have a different scheme in mind?

Yes, both the kiosk app and the tool will use Azure AD bearer tokens—exactly as in the existing system. The tool will validate tokens via Azure AD’s OpenID Connect metadata endpoint, using the `aud` claim to verify the audience is `https://wardnote-sync.it.hospital.local`, and the `roles` claim to check that the user has the `Nurse` role in the `Ward4B` group. Token validation will be done in a middleware layer in the .NET 8 Azure Function using Microsoft.Identity.Web, and we’ll cache the certificates locally for 60 minutes to reduce latency and dependency on external endpoints during peak hours.

Thanks, that's recorded: bearer tokens validated against Azure AD, checking the audience and the Nurse role, with certificates cached for 60 minutes. One planning question next. When does version one need to be in use on Ward 4B? This matters because a fixed date narrows what goes into the first release. If there's no fixed date, we'll plan without one.

We need version one deployed and in use on Ward 4B by the start of the next nursing shift cycle—October 15, 2024, which is a Monday. That gives us a hard deadline for all development, testing, and UAT, including training sessions for nurses. We’ll schedule a pilot rollout on October 14 for two 12-hour shifts and monitor for any issues before full deployment. This date is aligned with the hospital’s quarterly workflow optimization initiative, so we’ll prioritize features that must be in place by then.

Thanks, I've recorded the deadline: version one must be live on Ward 4B by Monday, October 15, 2024, with a pilot on October 14. That's the boundary we'll use to decide what goes into the first release.

Understood. We’ll scope the first release to include: nurse login via Azure AD, form entry for the 12 required fields, idempotent writes to both Cerner (HL7 ADT^A01) and the kiosk app (REST POST), a success confirmation screen, and logging of all actions with audit trail. Any additional features—like automated risk scoring, integration with FHIR, or multi-ward support—will be deferred to v1.1 after the October 15 launch.

Thanks for the first-release scope. One planning question before we go further: is there a budget range for this? It matters because it decides whether we build in-house or use existing hospital tools. If you're not sure, we'll leave it undecided.

Yes, the budget is capped at $180,000 for the full project lifecycle—development, testing, deployment, and six months of post-launch support. This includes personnel time, Azure resource costs (estimated at $12,000/year), and compliance validation. Since we’re using existing Azure resources and internal team capacity, we expect to stay well under budget. If we needed custom hardware, FHIR servers, or third-party HL7 gateways, we’d need to reevaluate, but we’re not—so we’ll proceed within the cap.

Budget noted: $180,000 for the full lifecycle, including six months of post-launch support, with Azure costs around $12,000 a year. Since you're reusing existing Azure resources and internal team capacity, I'll treat build-in-house as the default. Next, I'd like to know how many nurses will use the tool on Ward 4B, roughly, so we can size the expected load.

There are 18 nurses on Ward 4B—12 full-time, 4 part-time, and 2 on rotation—each working 12-hour shifts. On average, each nurse enters 3 to 5 ward notes per shift, primarily during morning and evening rounds. That’s approximately 60 to 90 notes per shift, with peak load around 30 notes in a 15-minute window during shift change. The tool must handle burst loads of up to 10 concurrent writes to both systems without timeouts or dropped records. We’ll size the Azure Function app to scale up to 20 instances during peak hours using Azure Monitor-based auto-scaling rules.
Thanks for the load detail. Next, roughly how many users will be on the tool at launch? This decides the scale and hosting defaults. If you're not sure, the default is under 100.

At launch, there will be 18 active users on Ward 4B, all nurses using the tool during their shifts. We expect up to 6 users to be logged in and active simultaneously during peak hours, so the system is designed for under 100 concurrent users. The Azure Function app will be provisioned with a standard tier plan (100 GB RAM, 200 GB storage) and auto-scale based on queue depth and CPU usage, ensuring responsiveness even during the 15-minute shift-change burst.

Thanks, that's noted: about 18 users at launch, up to 6 active at once at peak, designed for under 100 concurrent users. Next, the compliance question. This is health data, and it changes the hosting, data and security requirements. Which regimes apply here? The default, if you're not sure, is personal data under GDPR.

This is protected health information (PHI) under HIPAA, so we must comply with the U.S. Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, including the Security Rule and the Breach Notification Rule. Data must be encrypted at rest using Azure Storage Service Encryption with customer-managed keys (CMK), and in transit via TLS 1.3. All logs and audit trails must be retained for at least six years, and access to the data must be audited via Azure Monitor and Azure Sentinel. We’ll also comply with HITECH Act requirements for breach reporting and ensure that all data remains within the U.S. geographic region.

The participant has answered the compliance question, so I'm recording it and moving on. This is health data under HIPAA, with HITECH breach reporting, encryption at rest and in transit, six-year audit retention, and U.S.-only data residency.

Understood. The system will enforce data residency within the U.S. via Azure region locking (East US), use CMK for all storage, enforce TLS 1.3 for all external communications, and retain audit logs in Azure Log Analytics with a retention policy of 7 years to exceed the 6-year HIPAA minimum. All access to logs will require MFA and be triggered by the hospital’s SIEM via Azure Sentinel.

Got it: East US region lock, customer-managed keys, TLS 1.3, and seven-year audit retention in Log Analytics, with MFA and Sentinel access. Next, the people who use the tool. Who are the frontline nurses on Ward 4B, and what is the first thing each of them does when they open it?

The frontline nurses on Ward 4B are registered nurses (RNs) and licensed practical nurses (LPNs) with at least one year of hospital experience, all trained on Cerner and the bedside kiosk app. When they open the tool, the first thing they do is authenticate via Azure AD using their hospital-issued credentials—typically by scanning a QR code from the kiosk or entering their email and password on a touch-enabled tablet. After authentication, the tool loads their assigned patient list for the shift from Cerner via a FHIR Patient search (using the `practitioner` and `location` parameters) and displays a form for the first patient.

Thanks for describing the login step. Earlier you said charge nurses only review at handover and don't edit, and that ward managers and IT staff have no operational need. Before I record the users section, I need the charge nurse's first action. What does a charge nurse do first when they open the tool at handover?

At handover, a charge nurse opens the tool to review the most recent fall risk assessments for all patients on Ward 4B, but they do not enter or edit any data. The first action is to click the “View Summary” button, which pulls the latest 24 hours of notes from both Cerner and the kiosk app via FHIR Observation queries (using `code=fall-risk` and `date=last-24h`), then displays a consolidated list sorted by patient ID. This view includes timestamps, scores, and nurse initials, with red flags for any patient with a score ≥7 or a new fall event. No edits are allowed—only read access—and all views are logged with the user’s Azure AD ID and IP address.

Thanks, the charge nurse's read-only review at handover is clear. Before I record the users section, one thing needs confirming: when the charge nurse clicks "View Summary", does the list show all 18 nurses' patients for the whole ward, or only the patients assigned to the nurse who is on duty at that handover? That changes who can see which records.

Thanks, the charge nurse summary covers the whole ward. Users is nearly complete, so one more detail: do ward managers or IT staff ever open the summary, or is it only charge nurses at handover? Default: only charge nurses, and nobody else gets the summary. That means ward managers and IT staff have no access to it.

Correct—only charge nurses at handover can access the "View Summary" feature. Ward managers and IT staff have no access to the tool’s UI, including the summary view, and no path to view or query the data, even via admin portals. All access is governed by Azure AD role-based access control (RBAC), with only the `Nurse` role (restricted to Ward 4B) granted permission to use the application. The summary view is not exposed via any API or dashboard, ensuring no unauthorized access.

Thanks, that settles who can access the summary. Next I'd like to capture what a frontline nurse does in a typical shift, step by step, from opening the tool to finishing a patient's assessment. Walk me through one assessment as it happens on the ward.

A frontline nurse starts by opening the tool on a tablet at the bedside station, authenticates via Azure AD using their hospital credentials, and is immediately presented with a list of patients assigned to them for the shift—pulled from Cerner via a FHIR Patient search using their `practitioner` and `location` identifiers. They select a patient, then fill out the 12 required fields: fall risk score (1–10), mobility status, vital signs (BP, HR, RR, SpO2), skin integrity, cognitive status, and two free-text notes. After entering the data, they click “Submit,” triggering two idempotent calls—one to Cerner via HL7 ADT^A01 over TCP, and another to the kiosk app via a POST to `/api/note` with an Azure AD bearer token. The tool displays a success message with the timestamp and a unique audit ID, then automatically clears the form for the next patient.

Thanks for the walkthrough. One gap to close before we design the Cerner link: the spec doesn't yet define the HL7 endpoint, the message structure, or how errors are handled. Default: send an HL7 ADT^A01 message over TCP to a Cerner interface endpoint, with the request ID as the message control ID, and retry on NACK or timeout. That means the Functions app becomes a TCP client to a hospital interface engine, and duplicate messages are suppressed by the control ID. Should we keep that default?

Recorded: the Cerner integration will use the default HL7 ADT^A01 over TCP with retry on NACK or timeout, and the request ID as the control ID.

Now the user stories. Here is the core story as I understand it: "As a frontline nurse, I want to enter one fall risk assessment once so that it reaches Cerner and the kiosk app without re-keying." Does a nurse also need to correct or withdraw a note after submitting it, or is a submitted note final?

A submitted note is not final—nurses may need to correct or withdraw it if they enter incorrect data or observe a change after submission. The tool will allow a nurse to edit or delete a note within 15 minutes of submission, but only for the current shift. After that, the note is locked and can only be corrected by a supervisor via a separate audit override process in Cerner. The "Edit" action will re-submit the updated data to both systems, using the same request ID to ensure idempotency, and the kiosk app will update the record if the request ID matches. The "Delete" action sends a cancellation signal via a new HL7 MDM^T02 message to Cerner and a DELETE request to the kiosk API, but only if no subsequent audit trail has been generated.

Thanks, that clarifies the correction rules. Edits and deletes are allowed for 15 minutes, only within the same shift, and after that only a supervisor can correct the note in Cerner.

There is a conflict to resolve. You said a delete sends an HL7 MDM^T02 message, but Cerner-bound notes elsewhere in this spec use ADT^A01. Default: delete sends a cancellation as a separate message type, and the edit re-sends the same request ID. Should we keep that?

Recorded: a delete sends a cancellation as a separate HL7 message type, and an edit re-sends with the same request ID.

Next, the story for the charge nurse at handover, which isn't captured yet. Here is my draft: "As a charge nurse, I want to see every fall risk assessment on Ward 4B from the last 24 hours on one read-only screen so that I can review the ward at handover." Does that match what you need?

Yes, that matches exactly. The screen must display all assessments from the last 24 hours, sorted by patient ID, with each row showing the patient name, MRN, fall risk score, timestamp, and nurse initials. It must be read-only, with no edit or delete options, and include a filter for high-risk patients (score ≥7) and a count of total notes. The data comes from both Cerner and the kiosk app via FHIR Observation queries, joined by the unique audit ID, and cached for up to 5 minutes to reduce load on the backend.

Thanks, the charge nurse summary is captured. Now the functional requirements. From what you've described, the core capability is that a nurse records a bedside fall risk assessment once and it reaches Cerner and the kiosk app. Is that the first thing version one must do, or is there something a nurse needs to do before that, like picking a patient?

Thanks for confirming. Before the functional list, one gap: the kiosk integration doesn't yet define its endpoint, payload shape, or error handling. Default: POST to /api/note over HTTPS with an Azure AD bearer token, a JSON body carrying the same request ID and the 12 fields, and retry on 5xx or timeout with the request ID used for idempotency. That means the kiosk app is the second write target, and duplicates are suppressed by the request ID. Should we keep that default?
(I picked: {"type":"yes_no","value":true})

Thanks. The kiosk integration default is confirmed: POST to /api/note over HTTPS with an Azure AD bearer token, the request ID for idempotency, and retry on 5xx or timeout.

Now the functional list. Nurse records a bedside assessment and it is sent to Cerner and the kiosk app; nurse can edit or delete within 15 minutes of submission; charge nurse views the ward summary at handover. Let me take the first one further: when a nurse submits an assessment, what does she see on screen right after, and how long may that take?

After submission, the nurse sees a green confirmation banner with the message "Note successfully sent to Cerner and the kiosk app" and the unique audit ID, displayed for 8 seconds. The response time must be under 3 seconds for 95% of submissions, with a maximum of 5 seconds under peak load. If the system fails to reach either target, it shows a red error banner with a retry button and logs the failure to Azure Monitor with the request ID, but the form remains open for manual retry. The tool uses circuit-breaking logic to prevent repeated attempts during network outages.

Thanks, the confirmation screen and timing are clear. One thing to settle: when Cerner accepts the message but the kiosk app fails, should the nurse see the green banner or the red error? Default: red error with a retry, because the note is then not in both systems. That means the form stays open until both targets succeed.
(I picked: {"type":"yes_no","value":true})

Thanks, the default is confirmed: a partial failure shows a red error with retry, and the form stays open until both systems accept the note.

Next, the functional requirements are still not consolidated, and FR-3 and FR-4 are duplicates. Here is the proposed list to confirm:
1. Nurse records a bedside fall risk assessment and sends it to Cerner and the kiosk app (mvp)
2. Nurse edits or deletes a submitted note within 15 minutes, same shift only (mvp)
3. Nurse sees a green success banner with audit ID, or a red error banner with retry (mvp)
4. Charge nurse views the Ward 4B summary of the last 24 hours at handover, read-only (mvp)

Is this the right list, or is anything wrong or missing?

Yes, this is the correct core functional requirement list for version one. FR-3 already covers the feedback and timing behavior, and FR-4 is properly scoped as read-only, with no edit or delete access for charge nurses. There are no missing requirements—this list captures all essential behaviors: input, edit window, user feedback, and review. Anything beyond this, such as audit trail exports or real-time alerts, is out of scope for v1.0 and will be considered for v1.1 after the October 15 launch.

Confirmed: the four functional requirements stand as the version one core list, and audit exports and real-time alerts move to v1.1.

Now the business rules. You've already set the 15-minute edit window within the same shift. Here's an easy first check: when a nurse opens a patient who already has an assessment from earlier in the shift, should the form open blank, or pre-filled with the last values?

Recorded: a repeat assessment opens pre-filled with the last values.

One follow-up on that rule. Pre-filled values can be carried over unchanged into a new note, which could repeat a stale fall risk score. Default: the nurse must confirm or change each field before submitting, so nothing is saved from the old values by default. That means a new note always needs a deliberate save. Should we keep that default?
(I picked: {"type":"yes_no","value":true})

Confirmed: nurses must confirm or change each pre-filled field before a new note can be saved.

Next, a rule for the moment after a note is sent. If the 15-minute window closes while a nurse has the edit screen open, what happens to her unsaved changes? Default: the edit is blocked, the changes are discarded, and the nurse sees a message that the window has closed and a supervisor must correct the note in Cerner.

Recorded: if the window closes mid-edit, the edit is blocked and unsaved changes are discarded, with a message that a supervisor must correct the note in Cerner.

Let's go one level deeper on the same rule. A nurse opens a note at 14:58 and the window closes at 15:03 while she is still typing. Do the changes she made before 15:00 count, or does the whole edit fail? Default: the whole edit fails at the moment of submission, because the save is checked against the window closing time, not when she started typing.
(I picked: {"type":"yes_no","value":true})

Confirmed: the whole edit fails at submission if the window has closed by then.

Now acceptance criteria. Let's start with the simplest check for the first requirement: after a nurse submits a bedside assessment, how would a tester confirm the note reached Cerner and the kiosk app?

A tester would verify the note reached both systems by checking the Cerner interface engine’s message queue for an HL7 ADT^A01 message with the correct request ID, timestamp, and patient MRN, then confirming the corresponding Observation resource exists in Cerner’s FHIR server via a GET request to `/Observation?code=fall-risk&patient=MRN&date=eq[timestamp]`. Simultaneously, the tester would check the kiosk app’s audit log for a POST request to `/api/note` with the same request ID, the correct JSON payload, and a 201 Created response, and confirm the record appears in the kiosk app’s patient dashboard. All checks must pass within 10 seconds of submission.

Thanks, that gives a clear test for the send step. One part needs tightening: the Cerner check depends on an HL7 queue and a FHIR query, but the session states Cerner receives HL7 ADT^A01 over TCP. Should the tester verify Cerner only through the interface engine's acknowledgement (an ACK for that request ID), without a FHIR query? Default: yes, the ACK from Cerner is the proof of receipt, and the FHIR check is dropped from version one. That means the test passes on a received ACK within 10 seconds.
(I picked: {"type":"yes_no","value":true})

Confirmed: Cerner's ACK for the request ID is the proof of receipt for version one, and the test passes on that ACK within 10 seconds.

Next, the acceptance check for the edit requirement. Take a nurse who submits a note at 09:00 and edits it at 09:14. What should a tester see in the system right after she saves, and what should happen if the same save is attempted at 09:16?

After the nurse saves the edit at 09:14, the tester should see a green success banner with the audit ID, confirm the request ID appears in both the Cerner interface engine’s message queue and the kiosk app’s audit log, and verify that the updated data is reflected in both systems via their respective APIs within 10 seconds. If the same save is attempted at 09:16, the system should block the submission, show a red error banner stating “Edit window has closed,” and log the attempt with the request ID and timestamp—this is the expected behavior for post-window edits.

Thanks, the 09:14 and 09:16 cases are clear. One thing to tighten: the 10-second check for the edit mixes two verifications. Should the tester confirm the edit in both systems within 10 seconds of the save, the same as for a new note? Default: yes, the same 10-second limit applies to edits. That means a late or missing update in either system fails the test.

Recorded: edits must reach both systems within the same 10-second limit as new notes.

Now the technical section. The hospital subscription, resource group and .NET 8 stack are already set. The first decision is the API style for the kiosk-facing endpoint. Default: a single HTTPS REST endpoint, POST /api/note, protected by Azure AD bearer tokens, which matches what the kiosk app already calls. That means no new API protocol for the kiosk team to learn. Shall we keep that default?
(I picked: {"type":"yes_no","value":true})

Recorded: the kiosk endpoint is a single REST POST /api/note, protected by Azure AD bearer tokens.

Next, the retry behavior for that endpoint. If the kiosk returns a server error (5xx) or times out, should the tool retry the same request ID automatically, and if so how many times? Default: retry up to three times with exponential backoff, using the same request ID so the kiosk does not create a duplicate. That means the nurse sees one result, not a duplicate record.
(I picked: {"type":"yes_no","value":true})

Recorded: the tool retries the kiosk call up to three times with exponential backoff, reusing the same request ID.

Next, the same question for the Cerner side. HL7 messages are sent over TCP and the tool retries on a NACK or timeout, as already agreed. Should it also use one fixed request ID as the HL7 control ID for every retry of the same note? Default: yes, so Cerner can recognise a repeated message and not file it twice.

Before we wrap up, I still need your answer on the last point: should every retry of the same note reuse one HL7 control ID, so Cerner can recognise a repeat and not file it twice? I'll take that as the default unless you say otherwise.

Is there anything about this product we have not covered that a developer would need to know?

Yes—every retry of the same note must reuse the exact same HL7 message control ID (MSH.10), and the tool must generate a new sequence number (MSH.11) for each retry to comply with Cerner’s interface engine rules. The control ID is derived from the request ID, and the sequence number is incremented per retry attempt. This ensures idempotency at the HL7 level while maintaining message uniqueness for audit trails. Additionally, the tool must log the full HL7 message and retry count in Azure Monitor for every attempt, including the final outcome.

Thank you. Here is what I captured:

- Nurses confirm or change each pre-filled field before saving.
- Edits and deletes are allowed for 15 minutes, same shift only. If the window closes mid-edit, the whole edit fails and a supervisor corrects it in Cerner.
- Cerner's ACK for the request ID is proof of receipt. New notes and edits must reach both systems within 10 seconds.
- The kiosk endpoint is REST POST /api/note with Azure AD bearer tokens, retried up to three times with backoff.
- Cerner retries reuse the same control ID, with a new sequence number each time, and every attempt is logged in Azure Monitor.

Please tell me if anything here is wrong or missing.

summary:
The tool will run in a cloud account. Last Tuesday, a nurse in Ward 4B documented a patient’s fall risk assessment in both the hospital’s EHR (Cerner Millennium) and the bedside kiosk app (a custom app running on an iPad mini), re-entering the same 12 fields in both systems. The total time for this duplication was 1 minute 30 seconds per note. The tool must integrate with Cerner Millennium (via its HL7 v2.5.1 messaging interface over TCP) and the bedside kiosk app (via a custom REST API over HTTPS, using Azure AD Bearer tokens). The data model includes 12 fields: patient ID (MRN), timestamp, fall risk score, mobility status, vital signs, skin integrity, cognitive status, and two free-text fields for nurse notes. The tool will write to both systems using idempotent POST calls with a unique request ID to prevent duplicates.

Only frontline nurses in Ward 4B (registered nurses and practical nurses) use the tool regularly. Charge nurses occasionally review the records during shift handovers but do not enter or modify them. Ward managers and IT staff have no operational need to access the data through this tool. All nurse actions are automatically logged with timestamp, user ID (via Azure AD), and IP address for compliance with HIPAA and internal audit policies.

The participant will lead the development personally, working with a small team of two mid-level developers and one DevOps engineer. They will develop the tool using .NET 8 and Azure Functions, with code stored in Azure Repos, following the hospital’s CI/CD pipeline and infrastructure-as-code practices using Bicep. The tool will be deployed in the existing hospital Azure subscription under the IT Operations project namespace (project ID: IT-OPS-214), using a dedicated resource group named `rg-wardnote-sync`. This ensures compliance with centralized billing, network segmentation, and logging policies, and allows the application of existing security baselines. A private endpoint for the Azure Functions app will restrict access to the ward’s internal network and prevent public exposure.

The team knows .NET 8, Azure Functions, Azure AD bearer tokens and HL7 v2.5.1 well, has some FHIR R4 pilot experience, uses Bicep and Azure DevOps, and has no Node.js, Python or Kubernetes experience. So we'll build on the .NET and Azure stack. The kiosk app and the tool will use Azure AD bearer tokens, with the tool validating them via Azure AD’s OpenID Connect metadata endpoint, using the `aud` claim to verify the audience is `https://wardnote-sync.it.hospital.local`, and the `roles` claim to check that the user has the `Nurse` role in the `Ward4B` group. Token validation will be done in a middleware layer in the .NET 8 Azure Function using Microsoft.Identity.Web, and we’ll cache the certificates locally for 60 minutes to reduce latency and dependency on external endpoints during peak hours.

Version one must be deployed and in use on Ward 4B by the start of the next nursing shift cycle—October 15, 2024, which is a Monday. That gives us a hard deadline for all development, testing, and UAT, including training sessions for nurses. We’ll schedule a pilot rollout on October 14 for two 12-hour shifts and monitor for any issues before full deployment. The first release will include: nurse login via Azure AD, form entry for the 12 required fields, idempotent writes to both Cerner (HL7 ADT^A01) and the kiosk app (REST POST), a success confirmation screen, and logging of all actions with audit trail. Any additional features—like automated risk scoring, integration with FHIR, or multi-ward support—will be deferred to v1.1 after the October 15 launch.

The budget is capped at $180,000 for the full project lifecycle—development, testing, deployment, and six months of post-launch support. This includes personnel time, Azure resource costs (estimated at $12,000/year), and compliance validation. Since we’re using existing Azure resources and internal team capacity, we expect to stay well under budget.

There are 18 nurses on Ward 4B—12 full-time, 4 part-time, and 2 on rotation—each working 12-hour shifts. On average, each nurse enters 3 to 5 ward notes per shift, primarily during morning and evening rounds. That’s approximately 60 to 90 notes per shift, with peak load around 30 notes in a 15-minute window during shift change. The tool must handle burst loads of up to 10 concurrent writes to both systems without timeouts or dropped records. We’ll size the Azure Function app to scale up to 20 instances during peak hours using Azure Monitor-based auto-scaling rules.

At launch, there will be 18 active users on Ward 4B, all nurses using the tool during their shifts. We expect up to 6 users to be logged in and active simultaneously during peak hours, so the system is designed for under 100 concurrent users. The Azure Function app will be provisioned with a standard tier plan (100 GB RAM, 200 GB storage) and auto-scale based on queue depth and CPU usage, ensuring responsiveness even during the 15-minute shift-change burst.

This is protected health information (PHI) under HIPAA, so we must comply with the U.S. Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, including the Security Rule and the Breach Notification Rule. Data must be encrypted at rest using Azure Storage Service Encryption with customer-managed keys (CMK), and in transit via TLS 1.3. All logs and audit trails must be retained for at least six years, and access to the data must be audited via Azure Monitor and Azure Sentinel. We’ll also comply with HITECH Act requirements for breach reporting and ensure that all data remains within the U.S. geographic region.

The system will enforce data residency within the U.S. via Azure region locking (East US), use CMK for all storage, enforce TLS 1.3 for all external communications, and retain audit logs in Azure Log Analytics with a retention policy of 7 years to exceed the 6-year HIPAA minimum. All access to logs will require MFA and be triggered by the hospital’s SIEM via Azure Sentinel.

The frontline nurses on Ward 4B are registered nurses (RNs) and licensed practical nurses (LPNs) with at least one year of hospital experience, all trained on Cerner and the bedside kiosk app. When they open the tool, the first thing they do is authenticate via Azure AD using their hospital-issued credentials—typically by scanning a QR code from the kiosk or entering their email and password on a touch-enabled tablet. After authentication, the tool loads their assigned patient list for the shift from Cerner via a FHIR Patient search (using the `practitioner` and `location` parameters) and displays a form for the first patient.

A frontline nurse starts by opening the tool on a tablet at the bedside station, authenticates via Azure AD using their hospital credentials, and is immediately presented with a list of patients assigned to them for the shift—pulled from Cerner via a FHIR Patient search using their `practitioner` and `location` identifiers. They select a patient, then fill out the 12 required fields: fall risk score (1–10), mobility status, vital signs (BP, HR, RR, SpO2), skin integrity, cognitive status, and two free-text notes. After entering the data, they click “Submit,” triggering two idempotent calls—one to Cerner via HL7 ADT^A01 over TCP, and another to the kiosk app via a POST to `/api/note` with an Azure AD bearer token. The tool displays a success message with the timestamp and a unique audit ID, then automatically clears the form for the next patient.

The Cerner integration will use the default HL7 ADT^A01 over TCP with retry on NACK or timeout, and the request ID as the control ID. A submitted note is not final—nurses may need to correct or withdraw it if they enter incorrect data or observe a change after submission. The tool will allow a nurse to edit or delete a note within 15 minutes of submission, but only for the current shift. After that, the note is locked and can only be corrected by a supervisor via a separate audit override process in Cerner. The "Edit" action will re-submit the updated data to both systems, using the same request ID to ensure idempotency, and the kiosk app will update the record if the request ID matches. The "Delete" action sends a cancellation signal via a new HL7 MDM^T02 message to Cerner and a DELETE request to the kiosk API, but only if no subsequent audit trail has been generated.

The charge nurse summary must display all assessments from the last 24 hours, sorted by patient ID, with each row showing the patient name, MRN, fall risk score, timestamp, and nurse initials. It must be read-only, with no edit or delete options, and include a filter for high-risk patients (score ≥7) and a count of total notes. The data comes from both Cerner and the kiosk app via FHIR Observation queries, joined by the unique audit ID, and cached for up to 5 minutes to reduce load on the backend.

## Product overview and problem

### Product overview and problem

Nurses on Ward 4B currently enter fall risk assessment data twice, once into Cerner Millennium EHR and once into a bedside kiosk app. This duplication takes about 1 minute 30 seconds per note, including switching monitors. The tool aims to eliminate this double entry by allowing nurses to enter the 12 required fields once and have the data automatically synced to both systems. The solution must be deployed and live on Ward 4B by October 15, 2024, with a pilot on October 14.

## Target users and roles

### Target users and roles

- **Frontline nurse**: Registered or licensed practical nurse on Ward 4B; logs in with Azure AD; enters fall risk assessments for assigned patients.
- **Charge nurse**: Charge nurse on Ward 4B; reads the whole ward's summary of recent fall risk assessments at handover, read-only.
- **Ward manager and IT staff**: No access to the tool or its data.

## User stories

### User stories

- As a frontline nurse, I want to enter one fall risk assessment once so it reaches Cerner and the kiosk app without re-keying.
- As a charge nurse, I want to see every fall risk assessment on Ward 4B from the last 24 hours on a read-only screen at handover.
- As a charge nurse, I want to filter high-risk patients (score ≥7) and see a count of total notes in the summary.

## Functional requirements

### Functional requirements

This section describes the core capabilities that the product must deliver for the MVP. Each requirement includes testable acceptance criteria.

  - Acceptance: The screen is read-only, with no edit or delete options.

### Business rules

- The form pre-fills with the patient's last values during the same shift.
- Nurses must confirm or change each pre-filled field before saving a new note.
- Edits are blocked and unsaved changes discarded if the 15-minute edit window closes mid-edit; supervisors correct notes in Cerner.
- The edit window is checked at submission; if closed, the edit fails and unsaved changes are discarded.
- Edits must reach both Cerner and the kiosk app within the same 10-second limit as new notes.

## Technical requirements

### Technical requirements

The product will run in the existing hospital Azure subscription (`IT-OPS-214`) within a dedicated resource group `rg-wardnote-sync`, using .NET 8 and Azure Functions, with infrastructure as code via Bicep and source control in Azure Repos. Authentication uses Azure AD bearer tokens validated via OpenID Connect, checking the Nurse role in the Ward4B group. The Azure Functions app will use a private endpoint restricting network access to the ward's internal network. Retry logic is built for both Cerner (HL7 ADT^A01 over TCP with idempotent control IDs and sequence numbering) and the kiosk app (REST POST with Azure AD tokens and exponential backoff). Audit logs and full HL7 messages are recorded in Azure Monitor.

## Data requirements

### Data requirements

Capture 12 fields per fall risk assessment:

| Field            | Notes                              |
|------------------|----------------------------------|
| Patient ID (MRN) | Unique medical record number      |
| Timestamp        | Date and time of assessment       |
| Fall risk score  | Integer 1 to 10                   |
| Mobility status  | Enum or text description          |
| Vital signs      | BP, HR, RR, SpO2 (metric values) |
| Skin integrity   | Status description                |
| Cognitive status | Status description                |
| Nurse notes      | Two free-text fields              |

## Integrations

### Integrations

- **Cerner Millennium**: Writes fall risk assessments via HL7 v2.5.1 ADT^A01 messages over TCP, using the request ID as message control ID; retries on NACK or timeout.
- **Bedside kiosk app**: POSTs JSON to `/api/note` over HTTPS with Azure AD bearer token; uses the request ID for idempotency; retries on 5xx or timeout with exponential backoff.
- **Cerner patient list**: Pulls assigned patients via FHIR Patient search with Azure AD authentication.
- No FHIR Observation writes in v1.0; read-only summary uses combined FHIR Observations from both systems, cached.

## Security and privacy

### Security and privacy

- All nurse actions are logged with timestamp, Azure AD user ID, and IP address for HIPAA and internal compliance.
- Data encrypted at rest with Azure Storage Service Encryption using customer-managed keys.
- Data encrypted in transit with TLS 1.3.
- Audit logs retained for seven years.
- Access to audit logs requires MFA and is controlled via hospital SIEM with Azure Sentinel.
- Data residency is strictly U.S. only, locked to East US Azure region.
- Azure Functions app uses private network endpoint to prevent public internet exposure.

## Non-functional requirements

### Non-functional requirements

- Budget capped at $180,000 including six months of post-launch support; Azure resource costs about $12,000/year.
- Peak load expected up to 10 concurrent writes and about 30 notes in 15 minutes during shift changes.
- Designed for under 100 concurrent users, with up to 6 concurrent at peak on Ward 4B launch.
- Azure Functions app uses standard tier plan with auto-scaling based on queue depth and CPU usage.
- Response times: 95% of submissions within 3 seconds, max 5 seconds at peak load.

## Administrative surface

### Administrative surface

There is no operational need for ward managers or IT staff to access the tool or its data. No administration UI is planned for this MVP. Audit log access is provided through hospital SIEM tools and Azure Sentinel with MFA.

## MVP scope

### MVP scope

The MVP includes nurse authentication via Azure AD, entry of the 12 fall risk assessment fields, idempotent writes to Cerner (HL7 ADT^A01) and the kiosk app (REST POST), success confirmation with audit ID display, and audit logging of all nurse actions. Editing and deleting of notes is supported within a 15-minute window during the same shift. Charge nurses get a read-only summary view of all assessments on Ward 4B from the last 24 hours with filtering and note counts.

Deferred features for v1.1 include automated risk scoring, full FHIR integration for writes, multi-ward support, audit export, and real-time alerts.

### Implementation phases

The development is divided into phases, starting with the minimal end-to-end MVP slice and proceeding to expand features and stability.

### Phase 1: Core MVP Delivery

Goals:
- Implement nurse login via Azure AD
- Implement form for entering 12 fall risk assessment fields
- Implement idempotent writes to Cerner and kiosk app
- Display submission success confirmation with audit ID
- Implement audit logging of all nurse actions
- Allow edit and delete within 15-minute window and same shift
- Provide charge nurse read-only summary view of last 24 hours

Tasks:
- Develop Azure Functions API for note submission with HL7 and REST integration
  - Acceptance: API accepts note submissions with valid Azure AD bearer tokens
  - Acceptance: Sends HL7 ADT^A01 messages to Cerner with correct control IDs
  - Acceptance: POSTs JSON to kiosk app API with retry on failures
- Implement nurse authentication and authorization middleware
  - Acceptance: Only users with Nurse role in Ward4B group can submit notes
  - Acceptance: Charge nurses can access summary view
  - Acceptance: Ward managers and IT staff have no UI or API access
- Build frontend form with pre-fill and confirmation on each field
  - Acceptance: Form pre-fills with last patient values in shift
  - Acceptance: Nurse must confirm or change each field before save
- Develop note editing and deletion within 15 minutes
  - Acceptance: Nurse can edit or delete notes submitted in last 15 minutes of same shift
  - Acceptance: Edits re-send with same request ID; deletes send cancellation messages
- Implement charge nurse summary view
  - Acceptance: Shows all assessments in last 24 hours for Ward 4B
  - Acceptance: Supports filtering by high fall risk score
  - Acceptance: Displays total note count
  - Acceptance: Is read-only without edit/delete
- Setup Azure infrastructure with private endpoint, resource group and CI/CD
  - Acceptance: Deployment completes into `rg-wardnote-sync` resource group
  - Acceptance: Azure Functions app uses private endpoint
  - Acceptance: Automated builds and deployments from Azure Repos succeed

Phase acceptance:
- The tool is deployed to Ward 4B and live by October 15, 2024
- Pilot is conducted on October 14 for two 12-hour shifts without critical defects
- Nurses can submit, edit, delete notes successfully and see confirmations
- Charge nurses can view the ward summary read-only
- All integrations with Cerner and kiosk app function reliably under load
